title: Typhoon 24 is moving slowly; prepare for heavy rain before the weekend
summary: Typhoon 24 (Krovanh) is moving slowly north over waters south of Japan and is forecast to approach the Southwest Islands around September 4. Kahit hindi direktang tumama sa mainland, moist air feeding the autumn rain front can raise heavy-rain risk across wider parts of Japan.
why_it_matters: Slow movement increases the chance of prolonged rain and transport disruption in affected areas. The useful action is early low-cost preparation, not panic buying or assuming a specific landfall that is still uncertain.

sources.title: 全般気象解説情報（台風）

claims.text: JMA issued its third general weather information bulletin for Typhoon 24 at 05:44 JST on September 2, 2026.
At 09:00 JST on September 2, Typhoon 24 was south of Japan, moving north slowly, with central pressure 996 hPa and maximum sustained winds of 18 m/s.
claims.basis: Current JMA typhoon track data as reproduced by Japan Weather Association.

claims.text: The forecast track places the typhoon near the Southwest Islands around September 4, with slow or uncertain movement afterward.
claims.basis: Current forecast track and general weather guidance.

claims.text: Because the storm is slow-moving and can feed moist air into the autumn rain front, heavy-rain impacts may occur away from the typhoon's center even without a direct mainland landfall.
claims.basis: Meteorological inference consistent with the official broad-area heavy-rain guidance; exact local severity remains forecast-dependent.

content.key_message: Prepare now for possible heavy rain and transport disruption from September 3-6, but do not treat the current forecast as a confirmed mainland landfall.
content.what_changed: Typhoon 24 formed on September 1 and JMA has now escalated to repeated general typhoon guidance as the storm moves slowly north toward the Southwest Islands.
content.who_is_affected: Highest near-term concern is for Okinawa and Amami. People elsewhere in western and eastern Japan should watch local heavy-rain warnings because the rain front can be strengthened even away from the storm center.
content.when: Southwest Islands: around September 3-4. Broader heavy-rain risk can extend into the following days, with forecast uncertainty still high.
content.financial_impact: No defensible household yen estimate yet. Main avoidable costs are disruption-related: cancelled travel, flooded property/vehicles, emergency purchases and missed work if local warnings intensify.
content.risk_if_ignored: Waiting until warnings are already severe can leave less time to move a car from a flood-prone spot, secure outdoor items, charge devices, alter travel, or avoid roads exposed to flooding and landslides.
content.deadline: Do basic preparation by September 3; reassess using JMA local warnings before travel from September 3-6.
content.effort: Low: check JMA for your municipality, charge phones/power banks, secure balcony/outdoor items, confirm emergency supplies, and review travel cancellation rules.
content.potential_benefit: More time to avoid dangerous travel and unnecessary disruption costs if local warnings rise.
content.downside: The forecast track is unusually uncertain after the Southwest Islands; overreacting now could create unnecessary purchases or travel changes. Prepare cheaply first and escalate only when local warnings justify it.
content.what_to_do_or_watch: Use JMA municipality-level warnings and rain-risk maps rather than social-media track screenshots. If you have travel to Okinawa, Amami, Kyushu, Shikoku or other rain-prone areas this week, check airline/train cancellation rules before departure.
content.bottom_line: PREPARE now at low cost; change travel or evacuation plans only when local JMA warnings and the next track updates make the risk specific.
content.confidence_reason: High confidence that Typhoon 24 exists, is moving slowly north and has prompted JMA guidance; medium confidence on exact mainland impacts because the track after the Southwest Islands remains uncertain.
content.what_would_change_mind: A major eastward/southward track shift, rapid weakening, or removal of broad-area heavy-rain warnings would lower the recommendation. A stronger storm, slower movement, Level 3-5 local warnings, linear rainband forecasts or transport suspensions would raise it to DO NOW for affected areas.

reading_levels.30 sec:
What happened: Typhoon 24 is slowly moving north and is forecast near the Southwest Islands around September 4.
Why it matters: The storm can strengthen the rain front and cause heavy rain beyond its direct path.
What to do: Prepare basic supplies, charge devices, secure outdoor items and check JMA before travel September 3-6.
Bottom line: PREPARE cheaply now; do not assume a mainland landfall yet.
reading_levels.2_min: Typhoon 24 (Krovanh) is south of Japan and moving north slowly. JMA is issuing repeated typhoon guidance, while the current forecast brings the storm toward the Southwest Islands around September 4 and shows substantial uncertainty afterward. The practical risk is not only wind near the center: moist air can strengthen the autumn rain front and increase heavy-rain risk over a wider area. For most households, this is a PREPARE-not-panic situation: charge devices, secure outdoor items, confirm emergency supplies, check local JMA warnings and review travel cancellation rules. Escalate only if your municipality receives stronger warnings or transport operators announce suspensions.
